title: What are Spark's physical join strategies — Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ — small side broadcast to all executors, hash lookup, no shuffle of large side), Shuffle Sort Merge Join (SSMJ — both sides shuffled and sorted by join key, merge-step), Shuffle Hash Join (SHJ — both sides shuffled, hash table built on smaller side per partition), and Broadcast Nested Loop Join (BNLJ — for non-equi joins) — and how does the optimizer choose?
shortTitle: Spark's physical join strategies — BHJ, SSMJ, SHJ, BNLJ — and how the optimizer chooses

s1_definition.profdef: Spark has four physical join strategies. Broadcast Hash Join sends the small side to every executor, builds a hash table there, and probes it with the large side, avoiding any shuffle of the large table. Shuffle Sort Merge Join shuffles both sides by the join key, sorts each partition, and merges — the robust default for two large tables. Shuffle Hash Join shuffles both sides and builds a hash table on the smaller side per partition without sorting. Broadcast Nested Loop Join broadcasts one side and compares every pair, used for non-equi joins where no hash or sort key exists. The optimizer picks based on table sizes, the broadcast threshold, join type, and whether the condition is an equality.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India needs to match two lists. Broadcast Hash Join is photocopying the tiny branch list and handing a copy to every clerk, so each clerk matches their transactions locally. Shuffle Sort Merge Join is sorting both huge lists by account number and zipping them together line by line. Shuffle Hash Join is grouping both lists by account into buckets and, in each bucket, building a quick lookup from the smaller list. Broadcast Nested Loop Join is the slow last resort for fuzzy matches like "amount within ten percent," where you must compare every pair because there is no exact key.
s1_definition.oneliner: Broadcast for a small side, sort-merge for two large sides, shuffle-hash when one side fits memory per partition, and nested loop only for non-equi joins — the optimizer chooses by size, threshold, and join condition.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spark has four physical join strategies. Broadcast Hash Join sends the small side to every executor, builds a hash table there, and probes it with the large side, avoiding any shuffle of the large table. Shuffle Sort Merge Join shuffles both sides by the join key, sorts each partition, and merges — the robust default for two large tables. Shuffle Hash Join shuffles both sides and builds a hash table on the smaller side per partition without sorting. Broadcast Nested Loop Join broadcasts one side and compares every pair, used for non-equi joins where no hash or sort key exists. The optimizer picks based on table sizes, the broadcast threshold, join type, and whether the condition is an equality.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India needs to match two lists. Broadcast Hash Join is photocopying the tiny branch list and handing a copy to every clerk, so each clerk matches their transactions locally. Shuffle Sort Merge Join is sorting both huge lists by account number and zipping them together line by line. Shuffle Hash Join is grouping both lists by account into buckets and, in each bucket, building a quick lookup from the smaller list. Broadcast Nested Loop Join is the slow last resort for fuzzy matches like "amount within ten percent," where you must compare every pair because there is no exact key.

**One line to remember:** Broadcast for a small side, sort-merge for two large sides, shuffle-hash when one side fits memory per partition, and nested loop only for non-equi joins — the optimizer chooses by size, threshold, and join condition.

sections.s2_technical:
Broadcast Hash Join is the fastest when one side is small. Spark collects the small table to the driver, broadcasts it to every executor, and each executor builds an in-memory hash table from it. Then it streams the large table's local partitions and probes the hash table for matches. The large side is never shuffled, which eliminates the most expensive step. The requirement is that the small side fits in executor memory; the optimizer picks it automatically when the estimated size is below the broadcast threshold, and you can force it with a broadcast hint.

Shuffle Sort Merge Join is the default for two large tables. Spark shuffles both sides by the join key so matching keys land in the same partition, then sorts each partition by the key, then merges the two sorted streams, advancing whichever is behind. Sorting makes it robust to data that does not fit in memory because merging is streaming, and it handles large-to-large joins that broadcast cannot. The cost is the shuffle plus the sort, but it is reliable.

Shuffle Hash Join also shuffles both sides by key, but instead of sorting it builds a hash table on the smaller of the two shuffled sides within each partition and probes it with the other. It avoids the sort cost, which can be faster than sort-merge when one side per partition fits comfortably in memory. Historically Spark preferred sort-merge for safety because a too-large hash side can cause out-of-memory, and shuffle-hash is chosen only under specific conditions, controllable by configuration.

Broadcast Nested Loop Join is the fallback for joins that are not equality joins, such as a condition comparing amounts within a tolerance or a range overlap. There is no key to hash or sort on, so Spark broadcasts one side and, for each row on the other side, loops over all broadcast rows checking the condition. This is quadratic and slow, used only when nothing better applies, typically for small inputs or cross joins.

How the optimizer chooses, in order: if the join is an equality join and one side's estimated size is below the broadcast threshold, pick Broadcast Hash Join. Otherwise, if conditions favour it and a side fits per partition, Shuffle Hash Join may be chosen. Otherwise, for equality joins on large tables, Shuffle Sort Merge Join. For non-equality conditions, Broadcast Nested Loop Join or a cartesian product. Adaptive Query Execution can revise this at runtime using actual sizes, for example switching a planned sort-merge to a broadcast when a side turns out small after filtering.

A senior-level nuance is that size estimates drive everything, and bad statistics lead to bad plans — a missing or stale row count can make Spark skip a broadcast it should have done, or attempt a broadcast that blows up memory. So you keep statistics fresh, use broadcast hints when you know a side is small, and read the physical plan to confirm which strategy was chosen.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India joins a billion-row transactions table to a tiny fifty-row branch dimension. Shuffling the billion-row table would be wasteful. This is a Broadcast Hash Join — broadcast the tiny branch table and join locally with no shuffle of transactions.

Problem 2 — It joins the billion-row transactions table to the hundred-million-row accounts table on account id. Neither fits for broadcast. This is a Shuffle Sort Merge Join — shuffle and sort both by account id and merge.

Problem 3 — A risk report matches trades to price bands with a condition "price within five percent of a reference," which is not an equality. This is a Broadcast Nested Loop Join — broadcast the small band table and compare every pair.

The demo estimates both sides' sizes and the join condition type, applies the optimizer's selection rules, and logs which strategy it chose and why for each scenario.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four joins — transactions with a tiny branches table, transactions with a large accounts table, trades with a medium positions table that fits per partition, and trades with price bands using a non-equality condition.

Step 1: For transactions joined to branches, the selector sees an equality join and the smaller side is only four kilobytes, below the ten-megabyte threshold, so it chooses Broadcast Hash Join — the tiny branches table is broadcast and the huge transactions table is never shuffled.

Step 2: For transactions joined to accounts, it is an equality join but the smaller side is eight gigabytes, far above the threshold, and does not fit per partition, so it chooses Shuffle Sort Merge Join — both sides shuffle and sort by account id, then merge.

Step 3: For trades joined to positions, it is an equality join, the smaller side is above the broadcast threshold, but it fits per-partition memory, so it chooses Shuffle Hash Join — both shuffle, then a hash table is built on the smaller side in each partition.

Step 4: For trades joined to price bands, the condition is a tolerance, not an equality, so there is no key to hash or sort on, and it chooses Broadcast Nested Loop Join — the small band table is broadcast and every pair is compared.

Step 5: The demo logs each choice and notes that AQE may upgrade a sort-merge to a broadcast at runtime if a side shrinks after filtering.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:41:00 [INFO] transactions ⋈ branches -> Broadcast Hash Join (small side 4000 B <= threshold 10485760 B; no shuffle of large side)
2026-10-30 04:41:00 [INFO] transactions ⋈ accounts -> Shuffle Sort Merge Join (both shuffled + sorted by key, then merge)
2026-10-30 04:41:00 [INFO] trades ⋈ positions -> Shuffle Hash Join (both shuffled; hash table on smaller side per partition)
2026-10-30 04:41:00 [WARNING] trades ⋈ priceBands (within 5%) -> Broadcast Nested Loop Join (non-equi condition)
2026-10-30 04:41:00 [INFO] AQE may switch SSMJ to BHJ at runtime if a side turns out small after filtering.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  JOIN request
    │ equality join?
    ├─ NO → Broadcast Nested Loop Join (compare every pair)
    │
    ▼ YES
  smaller side <= broadcast threshold?
    ├─ YES → Broadcast Hash Join (broadcast small, probe local, NO large shuffle)
    │
    ▼ NO
  smaller side fits per-partition memory?
    ├─ YES → Shuffle Hash Join (shuffle both, hash on smaller per partition)
    │
    ▼ NO
  Shuffle Sort Merge Join (shuffle + sort both, merge)
    │
    ▼ (AQE may revise to BHJ at runtime)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spark has four physical join strategies and chooses among them by size, threshold, and the join condition. Broadcast Hash Join is the fastest when one side is small: Spark broadcasts that side to every executor, each builds an in-memory hash table, and probes it with the large side, so the large table is never shuffled. Shuffle Sort Merge Join is the robust default for two large tables: it shuffles both sides by the join key, sorts each partition, and merges the sorted streams, which is memory-safe because merging is streaming. Shuffle Hash Join also shuffles both sides but builds a hash table on the smaller side per partition instead of sorting, which can be faster when that side fits in memory, though Spark historically prefers sort-merge for safety. Broadcast Nested Loop Join is the fallback for non-equality joins, like matching within a tolerance, where there is no key to hash or sort, so it broadcasts one side and compares every pair, which is quadratic and slow.

The optimizer chooses in order. For an equality join where one side's estimated size is under the broadcast threshold, it picks Broadcast Hash Join. Otherwise, if a side fits per partition and conditions favour it, it may pick Shuffle Hash Join. Otherwise, for equality joins on large tables, it picks Shuffle Sort Merge Join. For non-equality conditions it falls back to Broadcast Nested Loop Join. Adaptive Query Execution can revise the plan at runtime, most commonly upgrading a planned sort-merge to a broadcast once it sees a side is small after filtering.

At the National Bank of India these choices were everyday decisions. Joining the billion-row transactions table to a tiny branch dimension was a broadcast hash join with no shuffle of the big table; joining transactions to the hundred-million-row accounts table was a sort-merge join; and a risk report matching trades to price bands within a tolerance fell back to a broadcast nested loop join because it was not an equality condition. The nuance I always stress is that size estimates drive the whole decision, so stale statistics cause bad plans — either skipping a broadcast that should have happened or attempting one that runs out of memory — which is why I keep statistics fresh, use broadcast hints when I know a side is small, and read the physical plan to confirm the strategy.
